chapters.title: Chapter 6: Risk, Tax and Getting Started

lessons.title: How Commodity Trading Is Taxed in India: Business Income, CTT and Losses

children.text: Rahul, a salaried software architect in Bengaluru, made ₹3 lakh trading MCX gold and crude futures last year. He assumed it was a short-term capital gain, like selling shares. It is not. Profits from commodity derivatives traded on a recognised exchange are taxed as business income, which means a different ITR form, different rules for losses, and possibly advance tax and a tax audit. Get it wrong and a profitable year can come with interest and notices; get it right and even a losing year can reduce your tax bill for up to eight years. By the end of this lesson you will know how commodity trading income is classified, how turnover is calculated, what CTT and other charges cost, how losses can be set off and carried forward, and the compliance dates that matter.

body.text: Commodity futures and options profits are not capital gains. They are non-speculative business income, taxed at your slab rate, reported in ITR-3, with expenses deductible and losses carried forward for up to eight years if you file on time.

body.label: A new Income-tax Act
body.value: The Income-tax Act, 2025 applies from 1 April 2026
body.context: It replaced the Income-tax Act, 1961, renumbering sections and using "tax year" in place of "previous year" and "assessment year". The core treatment of commodity derivatives described here carries over, but section references differ, so confirm current provisions with a chartered accountant.

children.text: Classification: Speculative or Non-Speculative?

markDefs.definition: A transaction in a commodity or share that is settled without actual delivery. Specific exceptions, including eligible derivatives on recognised exchanges, are treated as non-speculative.

children.text: Indian tax law treats a
speculative transaction

as one settled without actual delivery. But it carves out exceptions. Under the 1961 Act, amendments made in 2013 and 2018 treated eligible commodity derivatives traded on a recognised exchange, both non-agri and agri, as non-speculative. That treatment continues under the new Act.

columns.label: Speculative business income
points: Example: intraday equity trading, bought and sold the same day without delivery
Losses can be set off only against speculative income
Unabsorbed losses carried forward for 4 years
Carried-forward losses usable only against speculative income

columns.label: Non-speculative business income
points: Examples: commodity futures and options on MCX and NCDEX, equity F&O
Losses can be set off against income under any head except salary in the same year
Unabsorbed losses carried forward for 8 years
Carried-forward losses usable only against business income

body.title: Which head of income?
body.question: Sneha, a doctor in Jaipur, made a net profit of ₹1,20,000 from trading MCX silver futures during the year, holding each position for a few days to a few weeks. How is this income classified?
body.explanation: Commodity derivatives traded on a recognised exchange like MCX are treated as non-speculative business income, regardless of holding period. It is taxed at her slab rate and reported in ITR-3.

children.text: Calculating Turnover

Turnover for derivatives trading is not the total value of contracts you traded. Following the ICAI Guidance Note on Tax Audit, derivatives turnover is generally the sum of the absolute values of profits and losses on each trade.

body.latex: \text{Derivatives turnover} = \sum \left|\text{Profit or loss on each trade}\right|
body.caption: Add each trade's profit or loss ignoring the sign. Turnover matters mainly for deciding whether a tax audit applies.

body.title: Work out turnover
body.prompt: During the year, a trader closes four MCX trades with results of plus ₹40,000, minus ₹25,000, plus ₹15,000 and minus ₹60,000. What is the turnover for tax purposes, in rupees?
body.explanation: Turnover = ₹40,000 + ₹25,000 + ₹15,000 + ₹60,000 = ₹1,40,000. The net result is a loss of ₹30,000, but turnover uses absolute values.

stats.label: Tax audit turnover threshold
stats.context: Rises to ₹10 crore if cash receipts and payments are each within 5% of the total

stats.label: Typical threshold for online traders
stats.context: Because exchange trading is settled through banks, not cash

stats.label: Loss carry-forward
stats.context: For non-speculative business losses, if the return is filed by the due date

body.text: Turnover is not the only audit trigger. A tax audit can also apply in some cases where a trader declares a loss or low profit after having used presumptive taxation in earlier years. The rules interact in complex ways, so ask a chartered accountant to check your position every year.

children.text: Transaction Costs, Including CTT

markDefs.definition: A tax on the sale of non-agricultural commodity derivatives traded on recognised exchanges in India, similar to STT on securities. Designated agricultural commodity derivatives are exempt.

children.text: Commodities Transaction Tax
(CTT) is charged on the sell side of non-agricultural commodity derivatives. Designated agri commodities are exempt.

body.caption: Typical charges on an MCX trade (rates change; check your broker's latest charges page)

cells: Varies by broker; discount brokers often charge a flat fee per order or a small percentage, whichever is lower
Set by the exchange, a small percentage of turnover
On brokerage, exchange charges and SEBI fee

body.title: CTT on a Gold Mini sale
body.prompt: You sell one lot of MCX Gold Mini (100 grams) at ₹1,00,000 per 10 grams. What is the CTT at 0.01% of contract value, in rupees?
body.explanation: Contract value = ₹1,00,000 × 10 = ₹10,00,000. CTT = 0.01% × ₹10,00,000 = ₹100. Small per trade, but for an active trader these charges add up to a meaningful drag over hundreds of trades.

children.text: When trading is business income, these costs are deductible expenses. That includes brokerage, exchange charges, CTT, stamp duty and GST on charges, and can include genuine trading-related costs such as a portion of internet charges, trading software, data subscriptions and depreciation on a computer used for trading, supported by records.
Tax on Profits: A Worked Example

body.title: Show me the math: Rahul's commodity profits

children.text: Rahul is in the highest slab under the new tax regime because his salary is well above ₹24 lakh. His commodity trading shows:
Gross trading profit: ₹3,40,000
Brokerage, CTT, exchange charges, stamp duty and GST: ₹28,000
Trading software and data subscriptions: ₹12,000
Net business income: ₹3,40,000 minus ₹28,000 minus ₹12,000 = ₹3,00,000
Tax at 30% plus 4% health and education cess, an effective 31.2%: ₹3,00,000 × 0.312 = ₹93,600
If he had wrongly reported it as capital gains in ITR-2, his return would be filed on the wrong basis, and he would miss the deduction of expenses. A surcharge can also apply at higher income levels.
Losses: Set-Off and Carry-Forward
A losing year in commodity trading is not wasted for tax purposes, if you handle it correctly.

body.caption: Using a non-speculative business loss from commodity trading

cells: Set off against other business income in the same year
Set off against capital gains in the same year
Set off against income from other sources, such as interest, in the same year
Use carried-forward loss against future salary or capital gains
No, only against future business income
Carry forward if the return is filed after the due date
No, the right to carry forward is lost

body.title: What gets carried forward?
body.prompt: Priya, a salaried manager in Gurugram, has a salary of ₹15,00,000, short-term capital gains of ₹80,000 from selling shares, and a net loss of ₹2,00,000 from MCX trading. She files her return on time. How much business loss can she carry forward, in rupees?
body.explanation: The ₹2,00,000 business loss can be set off against the ₹80,000 capital gains in the same year, but not against her salary. The remaining ₹1,20,000 is carried forward for up to 8 years, usable only against future business income, such as future trading profits.

body.text: To carry forward a business loss, you must file your return by the due date. For individuals whose accounts do not need a tax audit, the due date is normally 31 July after the end of the tax year; for audit cases it is normally 31 October. Miss it, and the loss cannot be carried forward, even if it was lakhs of rupees.

body.title: The right form
body.textWithBlank: An individual reporting business income from commodity derivatives trading generally files ITR-___.
body.explanation: ITR-3 is for individuals and HUFs with income from business or profession. ITR-1 and ITR-2 do not cover business income.

children.text: Advance Tax

markDefs.definition: Income tax paid in instalments during the year on estimated income, rather than in one sum after the year ends. Shortfalls attract interest.

children.text: Trading profits usually have no TDS deducted. If your total tax liability for the year, after TDS, is ₹10,000 or more, you must pay
advance tax
in instalments during the year. Shortfalls and delays attract interest.

body.title: Advance tax instalments (cumulative share of estimated tax)

events.description: Full estimated tax for the year

body.title: The September instalment
body.prompt: Rahul estimates total tax of ₹93,600 on his trading income for the year, with no TDS on it. What cumulative amount of advance tax should he have paid by 15 September, in rupees?
body.explanation: 45% × ₹93,600 = ₹42,120 cumulative by 15 September. If he paid ₹14,040 (15%) by 15 June, he would pay a further ₹28,080 in September.

body.text: Trading income is lumpy. A single good month can create an advance tax liability that did not exist in June. Review your trading P&L before each instalment date and top up if needed, rather than discovering the shortfall in March.

body.title: The trader who skipped the paperwork
body.scenario: Aman, a 28-year-old consultant in Pune, traded MCX crude and natural gas for the first time last year. He made a net loss of ₹3,50,000. Since he lost money, he decided there was nothing to report and filed ITR-1 in December with only his salary. This year he is up ₹2,50,000 on commodity trading and assumes last year's loss will offset it.
body.prompt: What mistakes did Aman make, what are the consequences, and what should he do now?
body.modelAnswer:
Mistakes:
1. Wrong form. Commodity trading is business income, so he should have filed ITR-3, not ITR-1.
2. Not reporting the loss. Losses must be reported in the return to be recognised and carried forward.
3. Late filing. Filing in December, after the due date of 31 July for non-audit cases, means the loss cannot be carried forward even if reported correctly.

Consequences: he cannot use last year's ₹3,50,000 loss against this year's ₹2,50,000 profit, so the full profit will be taxable at his slab rate. His original return also misreported his income sources, which may need correction.

What to do now: consult a chartered accountant about whether any correction is possible for last year's return, keep full records of this year's trades and expenses, pay advance tax on this year's profits if his liability crosses ₹10,000, check whether a tax audit applies, and file ITR-3 by the due date this year.

body.title: Year-end tax checklist for commodity traders
steps: Download the tax P&L report and the full contract notes and charges statement from your broker.
Calculate net profit or loss and turnover as the sum of absolute trade results.
List deductible expenses with supporting records.
Check whether a tax audit applies based on turnover and your past presumptive taxation choices.
Confirm advance tax paid matches your actual liability, and pay any shortfall.
File ITR-3 by the due date, especially if you have a loss to carry forward.
Record carried-forward losses so you can use them in future years.

body.label: Income Tax Department e-Filing Portal
body.description: File returns, pay advance tax, view your annual tax statements and access official guidance.

Allowed against any income except salary in the same year.
Non-speculative business losses: 8 years, against business income only, if filed on time.
The return form for individuals with business income.

points: Profits from commodity futures and options on recognised exchanges are non-speculative business income, not capital gains.
Report them in ITR-3 at your slab rate, and deduct genuine trading expenses including brokerage, CTT and charges.
Derivatives turnover is the sum of absolute trade results, which mainly matters for tax audit applicability.
CTT is 0.01% on the sell side of non-agri futures and 0.05% of premium on options sold; designated agri commodities are exempt.
Business losses offset any income except salary and carry forward for 8 years, but only if the return is filed by the due date.
Pay advance tax on trading profits, and remember the Income-tax Act, 2025 now applies, with renumbered sections.

body.text: This lesson is for general education only and is not tax or legal advice. Tax laws, rates, thresholds, due dates and charges change, and the Income-tax Act, 2025 has replaced the 1961 Act from 1 April 2026. Individual circumstances vary. Consult a qualified chartered accountant before filing returns or making tax decisions.
